title: A-M-N

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ch-S-D: chesed, kindness, and the chasid, the kind one. Your line was a hasid is kind. What small kindness did you manage? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-two.

The battle is under way. Moses stands on a hill above it with his hands raised, and the story says that while his hands are up, Israel prevails, and when they drop, Amalek prevails. Arms get heavy. So Aaron and Hur bring a stone for him to sit on, and they stand one on each side, holding his hands up. Then comes a phrase that sounds like a small detail: "his hands were steady until the going down of the sun." In Hebrew, the word behind steady there is emunah. It's the same word that elsewhere gets translated as faith. Today's three letters live inside it.
screen: `MOSES ON THE HILL, HANDS RAISED.` → `FRIENDS HOLD HIS ARMS UP.` → `STEADY UNTIL SUNSET.`

segments.voice: A-M-N. Alef, mem, nun. Turn it four ways. First, steadiness. In the Moses story, emunah describes hands that don't waver, and they don't waver because friends are holding them. Faith here isn't an opinion. It's something that holds. Second, amen. The same letters give the word said in answer to a blessing. In Deuteronomy, as the Levites call out each line, the Torah says: "And all the people shall answer and say, Amen." To say amen is to say: this holds, I'll stand on it. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, offers a reading of amen as the first letters of three words, El melech ne'eman: God, faithful King. And in tractate Berakhot it goes further: the one who answers amen, it says, is greater than the one who says the blessing. Third, the craftsman. In the Song of Songs, a lover's beauty is compared to the work of a skilled craftsman's hands, and the word for craftsman there carries these letters too. A craftsman is someone whose hands you can trust: the joint holds, the seam stays shut. Fourth, people. When God describes Moses in the book of Numbers, the line is "who is faithful in all mine house." Faithful there is ne'eman, from the same root. Not a person with no doubts, but a person who can be relied on. So faith, read through these three letters, leans less toward certainty and more toward reliability: hands that stay up, a word that holds, work that doesn't come apart.
screen: `HANDS THAT STAYED STEADY.` · `AMEN: THIS HOLDS.` · `THE CRAFTSMAN'S HANDS.` · `FAITHFUL IN ALL MINE HOUSE.` · then, large: `FAITH IS STEADINESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say amen with meaning. Settle, and breathe. Let your hands rest, open, on your knees or on the table. Bring to mind one thing that has held for you: a person who keeps showing up, a habit that keeps you upright, a promise someone kept. Stay with it for a few breaths. Then, quietly or just inside, say one word: amen. Not as an ending. As a yes. This held. If you pray, you can answer amen to a blessing you know, slowly, meaning each sound. Then let the breath carry on. The bell holds the time.
A-M-N. Alef, mem, nun: the letters of emunah, faith and steadiness; of amen, this holds; and of the craftsman whose work holds. Today's word.
Your line: faith is steadiness. Today, the next time you say or hear amen, or simply say yes to someone, mean it the way a craftsman means a joint to hold. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Jews answer amen when they hear a blessing said by someone else, in synagogue and at the table, and the Talmud treats answering amen with care as a practice in its own right.

notes: Verses quoted from the KJV (1769), which the writer is sure of; JPS 1917 is believed to read the same in Exodus 17:12, Deuteronomy 27:15 and Numbers 12:7. A Keeper may prefer JPS 1917 wording; confirm.
Shabbat 119b (Rabbi Chanina: amen as El melech ne'eman) and Berakhot 53b (Rabbi Yose: the one who answers amen is greater than the one who blesses) paraphrased; confirm attributions.
Song of Songs 7:2: the craftsman word is biblical 'omman/amman'; the outline's 'uman' is the later/modern form. The script avoids naming the form; confirm.
Grouping emunah, amen, omman and ne'eman under one root follows the outline; confirm framing under the claims rule.
Exodus 17:11 says Israel prevailed while Moses' hand was raised; paraphrased with 'the story says'.
